clinicalPearls: Short stature is generally defined as height more than about 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, but the growth velocity and trajectory matter more than a single measurement.
The two most common causes are normal variants: familial (genetic) short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty.
Serial, accurately measured heights plotted on a growth chart are the single most valuable assessment, since a falling growth velocity is a key warning sign.
Bone age radiography helps distinguish constitutional delay (delayed bone age, preserved height potential) from familial short stature (bone age near chronological age).
A low or crossing-down growth velocity with poor weight gain suggests systemic disease or malnutrition, whereas short but proportionate growth with normal velocity favours a normal variant.
Endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency and hypothyroidism typically produce a child who is relatively overweight for height, in contrast to malnutrition or chronic illness.
Disproportionate short stature points towards a skeletal dysplasia and warrants assessment of body segment ratios.
Estimating mid-parental target height helps interpret whether a child's growth is appropriate for their genetic background.
reference.pathophysiology: Linear growth depends on an intact growth plate responding to growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1, thyroid hormone, and sex steroids, supported by adequate nutrition and freedom from chronic illness. Short stature arises when any of these are disturbed: genetic determination of a lower height potential, temporary delay in the tempo of maturation, endocrine deficiency, chronic systemic disease, undernutrition, or intrinsic bone/cartilage disorders. The pattern of growth velocity, body proportions, and bone age reflects which mechanism predominates.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Chronic systemic disease (e.g. coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, renal or cardiac disease)
Turner syndrome and other genetic/syndromic causes
additionalInvestigations: Accurate serial height and weight with growth velocity calculation
Screening bloods (full blood count, renal and liver function, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology)
Thyroid function and, where indicated, IGF-1 and growth hormone provocation testing
Karyotype or genetic testing in girls (to exclude Turner syndrome) and where a syndrome is suspected
Skeletal survey if disproportion suggests a dysplasia
redFlags: A crossing-down growth velocity or fall across major height centiles
Short stature with neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion
Disproportionate short stature suggesting a skeletal dysplasia
Poor growth with weight loss or gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting chronic disease
Dysmorphic features or other findings suggesting a genetic syndrome
reference.prognosis: Normal variants such as familial short stature and constitutional delay have an excellent prognosis with normal health, and constitutional delay usually reaches a normal adult height; outcomes for pathological causes depend on early identification and treatment of the underlying condition.
pitfalls: Relying on a single height measurement rather than growth velocity over time
Labelling a child as a normal variant without excluding treatable disease when velocity is poor
Missing an intracranial cause of growth hormone deficiency
Failing to consider Turner syndrome in a short girl
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause: recombinant growth hormone for growth hormone deficiency, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, a gluten-free diet for coeliac disease and optimisation of nutrition and any chronic systemic illness
Reassurance and structured observation for the normal variants of familial short stature and constitutional delay, with serial monitoring of growth velocity
Recombinant growth hormone for licensed non-deficiency indications such as Turner syndrome, SHOX deficiency and small-for-gestational-age children without catch-up growth
A short course of sex-steroid induction therapy for distressing constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Serial accurate auxology plotting height, weight and growth velocity, with bone-age radiography, to detect a falling trajectory
Referral to paediatric endocrinology with dietetic and psychological support as needed
Genetic evaluation and counselling where a syndrome or skeletal dysplasia is identified
